sheet.title: Happy Thanksgiving from Brennan’s, 3 Courses $80: choice of appetizer, entrée and dessert
sheet.line: Cheddar Grits, Piperade, Poached Egg, Debris
sheet.note: The sheet prints the dish name and its line and nothing else: no allergen marks, no price of its own (the $80 covers three courses), no method, no portion, no wine.

classic.grillades: Grillades, gree-YAHDS, are thin, pounded slices of veal or beef (pork in some modern recipes), braised in gravy until tender and served over grits at breakfast or brunch, a Creole dish; despite the name they are not grilled; the word is from the French griller; the cookbook grillades of the late 1800s were boneless veal medallions simmered in gravy (Wikipedia, Grillades; Saveur, Classic Grillades and Grits; New Orleans Magazine, A Royal Dish). A recipe for Grillades a la Creole ran in The Daily Picayune on 7 September 1898, and Grillades and Grits was on a breakfast menu in the Times-Democrat on 2 April 1900 (The Big Apple word history site, grillades). Carnival kings and queens still serve grillades and grits at krewe breakfasts after their balls (New Orleans Magazine, A Royal Dish).
classic.debris: Debris, DAY-bree in the pack’s lexicon, is the tender bits of roast that fall into the pan juices and gravy as it cooks and is carved, best known on the roast beef po’boy (Explore Louisiana, Roast Beef Po’ Boys with Debris; The Christian Science Monitor, debris po’ boys; the pack’s Débris term). Which roast gives the kitchen’s debris is not printed.
classic.piperade: Piperade is a Basque and Gascon dish of sautéed onions, green peppers and tomatoes flavored with red Espelette pepper; the name is from piper, pepper in Gascon and Basque; it is often served with eggs or ham (Wikipedia, Piperade; James Beard Foundation, Eat This Word: Pipérade; The Splendid Table, Classic Piperade).

sayIt: Debris: DAY-bree, as the pack’s lexicon gives it.
unsourced: What roast gives the kitchen’s debris, how the veal is cut and cooked, and whether the piperade carries Espelette pepper: asked of the chef.
A single origin story for grillades: the sources differ; only the dated newspaper records are used.
A view printed by a living New Orleans writer that cheese grits do not belong with grillades: left out, since it names a living person and is an opinion.
